title: Annotation-led SLI mapping and trace enrichment guide
content:
Purpose and scope:
This doc captures a pragmatic approach to pairing lightweight dashboard annotations with trace enrichment to make SLI investigation fast and repeatable. It focuses on token-serving inference flows (prefix warming, KV cache hits, model fanout, fallback variants) and on minimizing query costs while preserving signal fidelity for incident triage.

Goals (high-level):
- Normalize SLI definitions so dashboards and traces point to the same root signals.
- Define a compact trace enrichment schema so session reconstruction is cheap and reliable.
- Introduce an annotation convention for dashboards and incident timelines (human + machine readable).
- Provide a small SQL/snippet kit for deriving heatmap slices and SLI buckets used in runbooks.

Why this is different:
Many of our existing artifacts focus on metric taxonomy or deep tracing practices independently. This doc ties the two: annotations on dashboards are explicit keys used to trigger targeted trace captures and to auto-populate investigation decks. That closes the loop between operator workflows and backend sampling.

1) Canonical SLI mapping (compact)
- request_success_rate: 1 - (percent of requests with final status >= 500 or model_error)
  - source: request-level event (gateway logs) with status_code, model_error flag
- tail_latency_p99_token: 99th percentile of token emission time per request across the last 5m window
  - source: runtime token timing metric (token_emit_ms) aggregated by request_id
- median_path_latency_ms: median end-to-end from gateway receive -> response commit (for investigation comparisons)
- kv_cache_hit_rate: fraction of requests where prefix_kv_hit == true
- fallback_rate: percent of inference requests routed to fallback model variant in last 1h

Note: keep SLI names stable. The dashboard and alerting rules refer to these canonical SLI keys.

2) Trace enrichment key schema (minimal, flat)
Every trace should be annotated with a small set of attributes to make session stitching deterministic and cheap to index. These are stored as span attributes or top-level trace tags depending on tracer. Keep values short (no giant payloads).
- trace.session_id = <tenant-id>-<request-bucket>-<uuid-short>
- trace.request_id = <gateway-request-id>
- trace.route = <api-route-name> (e.g., /v1/generate-chat)
- trace.model_variant = <model-name>@<version> (fallback or primary)
- trace.kv_warmth = cold|warm|prefixed (enum)
- trace.kv_hit = true|false
- trace.batching_group = <batcher-id|none>
- trace.fanout_count = numeric (0 if single model)
- trace.seq_len = integer (input token count)
- trace.annotation_tags = comma-separated short tags used by dashboard annotations (see below)

Implementation notes:
- Use string enums for warmth/hit to avoid high cardinality. Avoid storing full prompt text in traces; store hashes only (trace.prompt_hash).
- For long-running multi-hop requests, set trace.session_id at first hop and propagate. Do not create a new root unless cross-tenant.

3) Dashboard annotation convention (human + machine)
Goal: When an operator annotates a dashboard (e.g., observed spike at 12:12), the annotation should embed structured keys to make downstream automation possible. Format: 
[OP-ANNOT|severity:low|tag:kv-cold|runbook:kv-warmth] Free-text note

Fields to include (optional but recommended):
- severity: low|medium|high
- tag: one or more short tokens (kv-cold, fallback, model-scaling, tenant-xxx)
- runbook: id of the runbook or play used (e.g., RB-2-KV-WARM)
- jira: optional linked ticket (ENG-####)

Example annotation: 
[OP-ANNOT|severity:high|tag:kv-cold,fallback|runbook:RB-2-KV-WARM] Suddenly large tail at 12:14, fallback spiked, tenant weight 0.8

How automation reads annotations:
- The annotation parser looks for OP-ANNOT prefixed notes, extracts tag/runbook, then triggers a targeted trace capture query limited to trace.annotation_tags contains any of the tags. This reduces the need for broad sampling or ad-hoc trace hunts.

4) Sampling and capture policy tied to annotations
- Default sampling: 0.1% traces per route for continuous sampling (low cost).
- Annotation-triggered window: when an OP-ANNOT is created with tag X on a dashboard, increase sampling for traces with trace.annotation_tags containing X to 10% for 15 minutes and persist one full session per tenant with full span logs (subject to PII redaction).
- Cost guardrails: cap annotation-triggered trace retrieval to 2000 traces per 15m window. If exceeded, fallback to random 1% sampling.

5) SLI heatmap slices and bucket definitions (SQL snippets)
Purpose: create quick-panels that break latency into operational slices. Use stable labels.
- Example slice query (pseudo-SQL):
  SELECT
    tenant_id,
    CASE
      WHEN seq_len < 64 THEN 'short'
      WHEN seq_len BETWEEN 64 AND 256 THEN 'med'
      ELSE 'long'
    END as seq_bucket,
    kv_hit,
    model_variant,
    percentile_cont(0.99) within group (order by token_emit_ms) as p99_token_ms
  FROM token_events
  WHERE day = current_date - 1
  GROUP BY tenant_id, seq_bucket, kv_hit, model_variant;

- Use these slices to power the dashboard heatmap where rows = seq_bucket, cols = kv_hit/fallback, cell = p99 token latency.

6) Investigation play examples (runbook snippets)
- Case: p99 token latency spike for tenant T around 10:03
  1. Check dashboard annotation timeline for OP-ANNOT entries near 10:03 for tags.
  2. Query traces using tag 'kv-cold' and tenant_id T for window 09:58-10:10. Use trace.session_id to reconstruct session.
  3. Confirm whether fanout_count > 1 or fallback_rate > 0. If fallback, escalate to model-oncall per runbook RB-3.
  4. If no fallback and kv_hit=false for many requests, suspect kv eviction or prefix mismatch. Correlate with cache-eviction metric and infra events.

7) Privacy and PII constraints
- Never index raw prompt text in trace attributes. Store only prompt_hash and optionally prompt_length.
- For traces marked with high severity annotation, ensure automatic redaction is applied to any captured spans containing potential PII (email-like tokens).

8) Dashboard UX recommendations
- Keep a top-level 'Investigation' panel with: top annotations (last 24h), top active tags, quick-runbook links, and a one-click 'capture traces for tag' button that opens a pre-filled trace query.
- Use limited cardinality dropdowns (tenant cohorts) instead of free text filters where possible to avoid explosion of panels.
- Show SLI baseline sparkline vs current window in each cell of the heatmap to quickly highlight regressions.

9) Ownership & rollout plan
- Owners: observability (primary), serving-runtime (secondary), console (UX).
- Rollout phases:
  - Phase 0: implement trace enrichment schema and enforce prompt_hash rule (2 weeks).
  - Phase 1: dashboard annotation parser + small annotation-triggered sampling (4 weeks).
  - Phase 2: rollout heatmap slices and operator quick-panel (3 weeks).
  - Phase 3: evaluate cost impact and iterate on sampling caps (2 weeks).

10) Open issues / TODOs
- Define canonical list of annotation tags (living doc).
- Small research spike: quantify additional trace storage for 10% annotation-triggered sampling on busiest routes.
- Confirm how on-prem/private customers want annotations handled (local only vs shared).

Appendix A — Short checklist for instrumenting a new route:
- add request_id and session_id to gateway logs
- emit token_emit_ms per token event with request_id label
- annotate kv_hit, kv_warmth at request root
- add model_variant as trace attribute
- ensure prompt_hash emitted but prompt_text suppressed

Appendix B — Example annotation parser regex
- regex: ^\[OP-ANNOT\|([^\]]+)\]\s*(.*)$
- parse key-value pairs by splitting on '|' then split each pair on ':'

Contact and feedback:
- If you plan to adopt this, ping @Ava Martinez in #observability and add a note to the rollout tracker (ENG-PRJ-obs-annot).

End of document.
